answer:
**Start with the retrieval problem.** Imagine recommending a video to someone learning guitar. The catalog contains millions of videos, so running an expensive neural network on every user–video pair is too slow. A two-tower model makes one vector from the user and another from each item. It scores a pair by a dot product: $s(u,i)=f(u)^Tg(i)$. Item vectors can be computed ahead of time and searched efficiently. A larger score means the model considers the pair a better match.

Training needs both a positive example, such as the guitar lesson the user watched, and competing items. A positive says “move these representations toward a higher score.” A negative supplies a comparison: “this other item should score lower for this user.” In implicit-feedback data, however, an unobserved interaction is not proof of dislike. That distinction becomes important when choosing negatives.

**What are in-batch negatives?** Suppose a batch contains three observed interactions: Alice watched Guitar Basics, Ben watched Football Highlights, and Cara watched Pasta Recipes. For Alice, Guitar Basics is the positive; the other two batch items are used as negatives. For Ben and Cara, the diagonal pairing changes accordingly. Compute the three user vectors and three item vectors once, then obtain all nine scores with one matrix multiplication. A batch of size $B$ supplies up to $B-1$ negative comparisons per user without encoding another $B-1$ items for each user.

![Original three-user batch: observed diagonal pairs and six reused negative comparisons.](/answer-diagrams/in-batch-negatives.svg)

This is computationally attractive. Its hidden assumption is about which items happen to appear in those batches. Batches sampled from interaction logs contain popular items much more often than a uniformly sampled catalog would. The original Google paper identifies this sampling problem in two-tower recommendation. [1](https://research.google/pubs/sampling-bias-corrected-neural-modeling-for-large-corpus-item-recommendations/)

**Why a Zipfian distribution makes this serious.** A Zipf-like distribution has a small popular “head” and a very long rare “tail”: an item's probability is approximately proportional to $1/r^\alpha$, where $r$ is its popularity rank. Imagine that Football Highlights accounts for 20% of logged interactions while a niche fingerstyle lesson accounts for 0.01%. In 100 independent negative draws, their expected appearances are 20 and 0.01 respectively. The niche lesson's chance of appearing at least once is only $1-(1-0.0001)^{100}\approx1\%$.

Consequently, the model repeatedly practices comparisons against the same head items while hardly seeing many tail items. A low training loss may mean “I beat the items this sampler usually provides,” not “I can rank the whole catalog correctly.” Popular items also receive many negative updates, and a popular relevant item can be incorrectly treated as a negative for another user. Do not reduce this to “the model always recommends popular items”: the direction of distortion depends on the objective, positive data, and sampler.

**A useful mathematical diagnosis.** Let $p_+(i|u)$ describe which items appear as positives for user context $u$, and let $q(i)$ be the negative-sampling probability. In an idealized contrastive identification problem—one positive among independent draws from $q$—the best discriminator compares the ratio $p_+(i|u)/q(i)$. Taking logs gives a score of the form

$$s_{uncorrected}(u,i)\approx\log p_+(i|u)-\log q(i)+c(u).$$

The $c(u)$ term is constant across items for one user and does not affect their ranking. The important extra term is $-\log q(i)$: the task learned from sampled competitors is different from directly learning the desired catalog probability. This idealized argument explains the source of bias; it is not an exact description of every real minibatch, where duplicates and correlated examples complicate the distribution.

**What LogQ changes.** A common training correction uses an adjusted logit $\tilde s(u,i)=s(u,i)-\log q(i)$ inside the sampled softmax. The sampler effect is represented explicitly in the training loss, allowing the underlying score $s$ to learn the intended probability scale rather than silently absorbing the sampler. Under this convention, retrieval normally uses the underlying score $s$, not the adjusted training score. The actual loss, temperature, and serving convention must agree. [1](https://research.google/pubs/sampling-bias-corrected-neural-modeling-for-large-corpus-item-recommendations/)

The same idea can be understood as importance weighting. If $j$ is drawn with probability $q(j)>0$, then

$$\mathbb E_{j\sim q}\left[\frac{e^{s(u,j)}}{q(j)}\right]=\sum_j e^{s(u,j)}.$$

The $q(j)$ in the sampling probability cancels the $1/q(j)$ weight. Because $e^{s-\log q}=e^s/q$, subtracting log-probability in logit space is equivalent to dividing by sampling probability before summing. This identity is exact for that sum; applying a logarithm or forming a ratio of finite-sample estimates does not automatically give an unbiased softmax gradient.

**Read the sign carefully.** With two raw logits both equal to 2, a popular candidate with $q=0.2$ has adjusted logit $2-\log(0.2)\approx3.609$. A rare candidate with $q=0.0001$ has adjusted logit $2-\log(0.0001)\approx11.210$. The rare candidate gets a larger weight *when it is sampled*, compensating for its rarity in the sampled sum. This is not an instruction to add 9.210 permanently to its serving score, nor a guarantee that its learned score increases. Larger negative logits can produce stronger negative gradients.

**Implementation details that change the answer.** Use the probability from the actual sampler. An interaction-frequency estimate is appropriate only when it represents that sampler. A per-draw probability $q(i)$ differs from the probability of appearing at least once in $K$ draws, $1-(1-q(i))^K$. Deduplication, expected sample counts, user-conditioned sampling, and temperature all matter. Most importantly, the positive item is included deliberately, not drawn as an ordinary negative. Recent work revisits standard LogQ specifically because treating that positive as another Monte Carlo sample leaves additional bias. Do not claim that a blanket `scores -= log_q` produces an exactly unbiased objective. [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331)

**Why hard-negative mining is a different tool.** For the guitar learner, an unrelated weather video may be an easy negative: its score is already far below the correct lesson, so training against it adds little information. An advanced guitar performance might be a hard negative if the task is specifically to retrieve beginner tutorials: it looks similar but does not satisfy the request. Mine candidates that the current model ranks highly, remove known positives and unsuitable comparisons, then train on the remaining confusions. Refresh the candidate index as the model changes; otherwise “hard” examples become stale. ANN-based mining is one way to find such candidates efficiently. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00808)

Hard is not synonymous with wrong. Another beginner tutorial could be a perfectly valid recommendation even if this user never encountered it. Penalizing it creates a false negative. Use known interaction history, multiple-positive labels, semantic duplicates, or human judgments where available; skip uncertain cases rather than treating all top-ranked unseen items as confirmed dislikes.

**How to combine the techniques.** Start with in-batch negatives for efficiency, add a sampled catalog component for broader coverage, and introduce checked hard negatives after the model learns basic structure. Mixed in-batch/uniform sampling has been studied directly for two-tower recommenders. [4](https://research.google/pubs/mixed-negative-sampling-for-learning-two-tower-neural-networks-in-recommendations/) If the sampler is a mixture, its probability is the mixture probability—not whichever component's popularity estimate is easiest to obtain. Deterministic hard mining may not supply a tractable sampling probability, so treat its objective explicitly rather than applying an unjustified correction.

Measure retrieval recall on realistic candidate pools, and report head, tail, and new-item results separately. A test containing only a few easy sampled negatives can make a weak retriever look excellent and can even reverse model comparisons relative to full-catalog evaluation. [5](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) Also measure false-negative rates, duplicate handling, and index freshness. Neither LogQ nor hard-negative mining removes exposure bias from the original interaction logs.

**The interview answer to remember.** In-batch negatives are cheap, but their item distribution inherits the logs' popularity skew. LogQ addresses the sampling distribution in the loss; hard-negative mining supplies informative comparisons. They solve different problems and are complementary. A reliable system also handles false negatives, documents the actual sampler, and evaluates on the distribution it must serve.
